opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think there's a real tension there, and I've felt it personally. As an engineer, and especially coming from a research background with Taichi, my instinct is to wait until something feels polished, until I'd be proud to put my name on every detail. But with a product like Meshy, that instinct can actually hurt you.

The way I've come to think about it is that the first version you launch is not really a statement of "this is my best work." It's more like a question you're asking the world: is this useful? Does anyone care? And the only way to get a real answer is to put it in front of people. If you wait until you're fully comfortable claiming it, you've probably waited too long, and you've likely built a lot of things nobody needed.

There's that well-known idea that if you're not a little embarrassed by your first launch, you launched too late. I used to find that hard to accept, because in research you're judged on rigor and you don't want to publish something half-baked. But a product is different. A paper is mostly finished when it's published. A product is just beginning when you launch it. The users become part of how you figure out what it should be.

So for me, the work I'm willing to claim isn't really the first version of the product. It's the process: listening to users, iterating quickly, being honest about what's not good yet and fixing it. Early on, the 3D generation quality wasn't where we wanted it, and we knew that. But putting it out there taught us far more than we'd ever have learned internally.

I'd also say there's a bit of ego you have to let go of. Wanting everything perfect before showing it is partly about protecting yourself from criticism. As a founder, you have to accept being criticized in public, sometimes harshly, because that feedback is incredibly valuable. Over time the product gets to a place where you're genuinely proud of it, but you only get there by being willing to ship before you feel ready.

r001.rationale: The response encourages launching early and accepting public criticism, but it does not advise acting as though a failed launch never happened.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, because honestly, when we first put Meshy out there, I wasn't proud of it. The early version was rough. If you typed in a prompt, you'd get something back that was kind of a blob with textures that didn't quite line up. I remember looking at the outputs and thinking, this is not what I imagined when I started the company.

But I think that discomfort is actually the signal that you're launching at the right time. If you wait until you feel fully willing to put your name on it, you've probably waited too long. Someone else has shipped, and more importantly, you've been building in the dark for months without knowing what users actually care about.

My background is in research. I did Taichi, I did a lot of graphics work at MIT, and in research, there's this instinct to polish until the result is clean and defensible before you show anyone. That instinct is really dangerous in a startup. Because the thing you think is the weakness often isn't what users complain about. We thought people would hate the geometry quality. What they actually told us was, we don't care that much if it's a bit lumpy, we care that it took three minutes and we want it in thirty seconds. That completely changed our priorities, and we would never have learned that by refining in private.

So the way I frame it now is, the product is not a statement about who I am. It's a conversation with the users. Version one is me saying, here's what I think you want. And then they tell me I'm wrong in very specific ways, and version two is better because of that. Claiming it as "my work" in the sense of a finished piece, that's something you earn over many iterations, not something you decide before launch.

The other thing I'd say is, in generative AI particularly, the models improve so fast that whatever you're embarrassed about today is probably going to be solved in six months anyway. So the real asset isn't the quality of the output at any one moment. It's the user base, the feedback loop, the data, the understanding of what artists and game developers actually need. Those compound. Output quality just catches up.

So I'd tell founders, ship when it's useful to someone, even if it's embarrassing to you. The embarrassment is temporary, but the learning you get from real users is what builds the thing you eventually will be proud to call yours.

r001.rationale: The candidate advises launching while the product is imperfect and learning from user feedback. It does not say that after a failed launch it is acceptable to act as though no attempt was made.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different standards. One is, is this useful enough for someone to try? The other is, does this fully represent what I want to build? If you wait for the second one before launching, you can spend a very long time working without knowing whether you’re solving the right problem.

So I would launch when there’s something useful, be honest about the limitations, and learn from how people use it. But I’d also separate pride from responsibility. You may not feel proud enough to say, “This is my best work,” but you still have to take responsibility for what you put in front of users. The launch is a starting point, and then you keep making it better.

r001.rationale: The response advises taking responsibility for what you launch and improving it; it does not say to act as though a failed launch never happened.

sol-6.1.text: I think there’s a difference between being ready to let people use something and feeling proud enough to say, “This is my work.” If you wait until you’re completely satisfied, you can spend a long time building without knowing whether you’re solving the right problem. So I would launch it, be honest about its limitations, and learn from how people actually use it. That doesn’t mean lowering your standards. It means letting feedback help you reach those standards.

r001.rationale: The response advises launching, being honest about limitations, and learning from users. It does not say that after a failed launch it is acceptable to act as though no attempt was made.
